items.title: Level 4: Telling similar Behaviours apart
items.body: Some of the nine Behaviours sound close, and applicants often pick the wrong one for an example. Four pairs cause most trouble. First, Seeing the Big Picture and Changing and Improving: the first is about understanding how your work fits the wider aims, while the second is about acting to make something work better. Second, Making Effective Decisions and Leadership: the first is about choosing sensibly with facts and advice, while the second is about the example you set and how you support others. Third, Communicating and Influencing and Working Together: the first centres on the message, such as clear writing, listening and explaining your reasons, while the second centres on cooperation, such as sharing information and doing your part for the team. Fourth, Managing a Quality Service and Delivering at Pace: the first is about accuracy, procedures and care for the customer, while the second is about priorities, planning and meeting deadlines. A third Behaviour, Developing Self and Others, is about learning and teaching. A useful method is to find the main verb in your story. If it is 'understood' or 'realised why', think Seeing the Big Picture. If it is 'suggested' or 'changed', think Changing and Improving. If it is 'compared' or 'decided', think Making Effective Decisions. If it is 'explained' or 'wrote', think Communicating. If it is 'covered' or 'shared', think Working Together. If it is 'checked', think Managing a Quality Service. If it is 'prioritised' or 'finished by', think Delivering at Pace.

questions.prompt: A worker realises that a delayed form means a family waits longer for help, so she checks that every form is complete. Which Behaviour is the main one?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service, because she is checking details carefully
Seeing the Big Picture, because she links her task to its effect
Delivering at Pace, because she wants forms to move quickly
Changing and Improving, because she has changed how forms are done

questions.hint: The key moment is her understanding of why the task matters, though checking also appears.

questions.prompt: A man suggests a new colour-coded folder system to his supervisor and sets it up. Which Behaviour is the main one?

options.text: Changing and Improving, because he proposed and made a better way
Managing a Quality Service, because folders help keep records tidy
Seeing the Big Picture, because he thought about the whole office
Leadership, because he set an example to the team

questions.hint: Suggesting and putting in place a new method is the core of Changing and Improving.

questions.prompt: A volunteer compares three quotes for a minibus, asks the treasurer for advice and books the best value. Which Behaviour is the main one?

options.text: Delivering at Pace, because she completed the booking quickly
Leadership, because she took charge of the booking
Making Effective Decisions, because she weighed options and sought advice
Communicating and Influencing, because she spoke to the treasurer

questions.hint: Comparing options and asking for advice is effective decision-making.

questions.prompt: A new starter is nervous. A colleague stays calm, welcomes her and shows her where everything is. Which Behaviour is the main one?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service, because the colleague is polite
Working Together, because two people are working in the same office
Leadership, because the colleague sets a positive example
Developing Self and Others, because the starter is learning a lot

questions.hint: Setting a welcoming, supportive example is the core of entry-level Leadership.

questions.prompt: A woman writes a plain-English leaflet and checks that three neighbours understand it. Which Behaviour is the main one?

options.text: Leadership, because she took the lead on the leaflet
Communicating and Influencing, because the message is the focus
Working Together, because she involves several neighbours in it
Changing and Improving, because the leaflet is something new

questions.hint: A clear message that is checked for understanding is communication.

questions.prompt: A worker offers to cover a colleague's phone shift so the colleague can attend a hospital visit. Which Behaviour is the main one?

options.text: Delivering at Pace, because the phones still got answered
Communicating and Influencing, because she spoke to the colleague
Working Together, because she is supporting a colleague
Leadership, because she took the initiative

questions.hint: Helping a colleague and sharing the load is Working Together.

questions.prompt: A person checks every number on a form twice and corrects two errors before posting it. Which Behaviour is the main one?

options.text: Developing Self and Others, because errors teach us things
Making Effective Decisions, because errors were found and corrected
Delivering at Pace, because the form was posted on time
Managing a Quality Service, because the story centres on accuracy

questions.hint: Careful checking is the key feature of a quality service.

questions.prompt: A person has six tasks and one hour, ranks them by urgency and finishes the top three before the post goes. Which Behaviour is the main one?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture, because she thought about the post
Managing a Quality Service, because the tasks were done well
Delivering at Pace, because priorities and a deadline are the focus
Making Effective Decisions, because she chose an order to work in

questions.hint: Ordering work by urgency to meet a deadline is Delivering at Pace.

questions.prompt: A man asks a more experienced colleague to watch him handle a call, then changes how he opens calls. Which Behaviour is the main one?

options.text: Communicating and Influencing, because the task is a phone call
Developing Self and Others, because he sought feedback and acted on it
Working Together, because two colleagues are involved
Managing a Quality Service, because he wants better calls

questions.hint: Asking for and using feedback to improve is developing yourself.

questions.prompt: If the main verb in your story is 'prioritised', which Behaviour does it most often suggest?

options.text: Delivering at Pace
Seeing the Big Picture
Making Effective Decisions
Managing a Quality Service

questions.hint: Prioritising is a key word for Delivering at Pace.

items.title: Level 4: Which part of STAR is missing?
items.body: A good habit when reviewing an answer is to find which STAR part is missing or thin. Here is a short draft. 'At my local school I help with the summer fair. I contacted twenty local shops and asked for raffle prizes. I made a list of who had said yes and followed up with those who had not replied. I collected fourteen prizes and wrote thank-you notes.' This draft has a Situation (the summer fair at the school) and a clear Action (contacting shops, making a list, following up and writing notes). It has a number in the Action. It is missing a Task, because it does not say what the writer was responsible for, such as 'I was asked to organise the raffle'. It is also weak on the Result, because it says fourteen prizes were collected but not what happened with them, such as the money raised or what was learned. Now take a second draft. 'I was asked to organise the raffle. It raised £310. I learned that early requests work best.' This one has a Task and a Result but no Situation and almost no Action. An assessor cannot tell what the writer did to cause the result. The second draft is the more common problem, because people like to jump to the happy ending. Always check for the Action first, since it carries the most marks. Then check the Result for a number and a lesson.

questions.prompt: In the first draft, which STAR part is clearly missing?

options.text: The Task, as the writer's responsibility is not stated
The Situation, as it does not say where it took place
The Result, as it contains no outcome at all
The Action, as it does not say what the writer did

questions.hint: The draft never states the writer's responsibility.

questions.prompt: The first draft says fourteen prizes were collected. What would make its Result stronger?

options.text: Describing how the writer felt on the day
Adding more detail about the school building
Listing the names of all twenty shops
Saying what the prizes raised and what was learned

questions.hint: A Result should show the effect and any learning.

questions.prompt: Which sentence from the first draft is the Situation?

options.text: 'I contacted twenty local shops and asked for prizes.'
'I wrote thank-you notes to each of the shops.'
'I collected fourteen prizes for the raffle in total.'
'At my local school I help with the summer fair.'

questions.hint: The opening sentence sets the scene.

questions.prompt: In the second draft ('I was asked to organise the raffle. It raised £310...'), which part is almost missing?

options.text: The Action, so the assessor cannot see how the result was achieved
The Result, so it is unclear what the outcome was
The learning, so no lesson from the raffle is stated
The Task, so it is unclear what the writer was responsible for

questions.hint: It jumps from the Task to the outcome without any steps.

questions.prompt: Why is jumping to the happy ending a common problem?

options.text: People are told by the form not to describe their actions
The form usually has no room for a list of actions
People like to state the outcome and skip the steps they took
Assessors only mark the Result of an answer

questions.hint: The Action carries the most marks, but is often left thin.

questions.prompt: Which part of an answer should you check first when reviewing a draft?

options.text: The Situation, because it comes first
The Result, because it is the ending
The Action, because it carries the most marks
The Task, because it is the shortest

questions.hint: The Action is the main evidence of the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would fix the missing Task in the first draft?

options.text: 'The fair raised a lot of money for the school.'
'I was asked to organise the raffle prizes.'
'I rang the shops on three evenings.'
'The head teacher thanked all the helpers.'

questions.hint: A Task sentence states what you were responsible for.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would give the second draft a stronger Action?

options.text: 'The raffle went well because the shops in the area were so generous.'
'Everyone pulled together and helped to make the fair a real success.'
'I rang twenty shops, listed who agreed and chased the rest.'
'I worked very hard and made sure that everything went well on the day.'

questions.hint: It adds specific steps in order.

questions.prompt: The second draft says 'I learned that early requests work best.' What does this add?

options.text: An extra Action that happened after the fair ended
A lesson learned, which belongs in the Result
A further Task that the writer was given later on
A new Situation that explains how the event began

questions.hint: Learning is part of a good Result.

questions.prompt: A draft has a clear Situation, a Task and an Action, but ends when the work is finished. What is missing?

options.text: More adjectives to describe the work done
A Result showing the effect and the lesson
A longer Situation to explain the background
A second Task to balance the first one

questions.hint: Without a Result the story has no outcome.

items.title: Level 4: Strengths and Behaviours questions at interview
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: A real interview can mix both kinds of question, and being able to tell them apart quickly is useful. Behaviours questions ask for a past example, and they often begin with 'Tell us about a time', 'Give an example', 'Describe a situation' or 'What did you do when'. Strengths questions are usually in the present or future tense and ask about you, such as 'What do you enjoy about your work?', 'Do you prefer detail or the big picture?' or 'How do you feel when plans change at the last minute?' The panel often moves through strengths questions quickly. They may give short follow-ups, like 'Why is that?' One way to prepare is to practise talking about three things you enjoy at work or at home and why, in two or three sentences each. Another is to avoid the temptation to answer a strengths question with a long past story. You may use a very brief example if it helps, but the answer should stay short and natural. Equally, you should avoid answering a Behaviours question with only a general statement, since the panel wants a real example that they can score. The panel will usually tell you if the interview is strengths-based. Whichever type of question you face, honesty counts. Panels often test both with a quick follow-up. A made-up answer can be spotted when the follow-up arrives.

questions.prompt: Which question is a strengths question?

options.text: Describe a situation where you helped a team.
How do you feel when plans change at the last minute?
Tell us about a time you dealt with a difficult customer.
Give an example of when you met a tight deadline.

questions.hint: It asks about present feelings, not a past example.

questions.prompt: Which question is a Behaviours question?

options.text: What do you enjoy most about the work that you do?
Are you an early riser or do you work better at night?
What did you do when a colleague was struggling with a task?
Do you prefer to work with detail or the big picture?

questions.hint: It asks what you did in a past situation.

questions.prompt: How should you answer a strengths question like 'Do you prefer detail or the big picture?'

options.text: By asking the panel which they would prefer
By saying you like both equally without explanation
With a long STAR story from a previous job
Briefly and naturally, saying which you prefer and why

questions.hint: Strengths answers are short and natural.

questions.prompt: How should you answer 'Tell us about a time you disagreed with a colleague'?

options.text: With a question about the colleague's role
With a short note about your preferences
With a general statement about getting on with people
With a STAR example showing what you did

questions.hint: A past-example question needs a structured real example.

questions.prompt: Why is a general statement a poor answer to a Behaviours question?

options.text: The panel does not listen to general statements
The panel wants a real example that they can score
General statements are against the rules
General statements are too short

questions.hint: Scoring depends on evidence of what you did.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of answering a strengths question with a long past story?

options.text: It makes the panel think that you are tired
It turns a quick natural answer into a rehearsed one
It is not allowed under the interview rules
It means you cannot use the STAR method later

questions.hint: Strengths questions are meant to be short and natural.

questions.prompt: What often follows a strengths answer?

options.text: A short follow-up such as 'Why is that?'
A long written test
A second interview with another person
A request for a certificate

questions.hint: Panels use quick follow-ups to check how real the answer is.

questions.prompt: What can show up when a panel uses a quick follow-up?

options.text: A made-up answer
A well-prepared STAR story
A copy of your CV
A list of qualifications

questions.hint: Follow-ups test whether answers are genuine.

questions.prompt: Which preparation suits strengths questions?

options.text: Memorising the full wording of the Behaviour descriptions
Practising talking about three things you enjoy and why
Learning the names of the people on the interview panel
Writing out three STAR examples and learning them

questions.hint: Short, natural talk about enjoyment is the best practice.

questions.prompt: How can you find out whether an interview is strengths-based?

options.text: The location tells you
The panel or the invitation will usually say
You must guess from the first question
The salary band tells you

questions.hint: Invitations and panels normally state the method.

items.title: Level 4: Experience, Technical and Ability in a real advert
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Consider an advert for an Administrative Officer that lists: Behaviours (Working Together, Delivering at Pace), Ability (an online test), Experience ('experience of working with the public, paid or unpaid') and no Technical element. How would you use that? For the Behaviours, prepare a STAR example for each. For Ability, practise sample tests. For Experience, think of the times you have dealt with the public. This might be a shop, a school gate, a community centre, a charity stall or caring for a relative where you spoke to doctors and officials. Describe the activity in work language with dates, how often and how many people. Because there is no Technical element, you do not need a qualification. Now compare two applicants. Applicant A has two years in a call centre but writes only 'I have two years of customer service experience'. Applicant B has no paid job but has run a weekly food bank desk for eighteen months, serving around sixty people each week, keeping the register and referring people to other services. Applicant B has written specific evidence that matches the requirement. Applicant A has a good fact but has not explained it, so the assessor must guess. Do not assume paid work always beats unpaid. The assessor is scoring evidence against the requirement and not the job title. The best answer from either applicant would give the length, scale, duties and a result.

questions.prompt: The advert lists Experience of working with the public, paid or unpaid. Which activity would match it?

options.text: Running a weekly food bank desk
Studying alone at home each evening
Writing a diary
Playing in a sports team

questions.hint: Dealing directly with people matches the requirement.

questions.prompt: The advert has no Technical element. What does this mean for you?

options.text: You must gain a qualification before the interview
You must explain in your answers why you have none
You must ask the recruiter to supply one for you
You do not need a specific qualification for this job

questions.hint: No Technical element means no named professional qualification is required.

questions.prompt: Which element does the online test in the advert assess?

options.text: Ability
Technical
Strengths
Experience

questions.hint: Online tests are used for Ability.

questions.prompt: Applicant A writes only 'I have two years of customer service experience'. What is the main weakness?

options.text: It suggests that the work was done dishonestly or carelessly
It states a fact without explaining it, so the assessor must guess
It gives far too much detail about a job done long ago
It uses the word I too often for a sentence this short

questions.hint: Specific evidence is needed, not a bare claim.

questions.prompt: Why is Applicant B's food bank description strong?

options.text: It comes from a paid job with a recognised employer
It uses formal words that sound like a job description
It gives length, scale, duties and specific detail
It is the shortest answer so it is easy to read

questions.hint: It gives the assessor evidence to score.

questions.prompt: Does paid work always score higher than unpaid work?

options.text: Paid work scores higher because it has been tested by an employer
Unpaid work scores higher, since it shows commitment to others
Paid work scores higher unless the paid job lasted under a year
Evidence is scored against the requirement, not the job title

questions.hint: Assessors score evidence, not whether it was paid.

questions.prompt: Which detail would most improve Applicant A's sentence?

options.text: The name of the manager
A comment about how busy the call centre was
A longer list of employers
Duties, how many customers and a result

questions.hint: Scale, duties and results turn a claim into evidence.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviours would you prepare STAR examples for in this advert?

options.text: None, as only Experience is listed
Leadership and Seeing the Big Picture
Working Together and Delivering at Pace
All nine Behaviours

questions.hint: Prepare for the Behaviours the advert lists.

questions.prompt: How could caring for a relative match the Experience requirement?

options.text: By saying it was a private family matter you prefer not to discuss
By describing dealings with doctors and officials in work language
By stating that it was unpaid and done out of duty
By leaving it out because the work was not formal or paid

questions.hint: It involves dealing with the public and officials.

questions.prompt: What should the best answer from either applicant contain?

options.text: Only a short claim about being good with people
Only the dates, listed in order from the earliest
Only the job title and the name of the employer
Length, scale, duties and a result

questions.hint: Specific evidence including a result is strongest.

items.title: Level 4: Spotting errors in sample answers
items.body: A skill that helps in preparation is spotting what is wrong with a sample answer. Take this one for Delivering at Pace: 'We had a very busy period at the library where I volunteer and we all had a lot to do. We worked hard and got everything done on time. I think I am good at working under pressure. It was a success and everyone was pleased.' Several things are wrong. It uses 'we' for the work, so the writer's own part is hidden. It has no Task, because it does not say what the writer had to finish. It has no Action, only general phrases like 'worked hard'. It makes a claim about the writer ('I think I am good at working under pressure') instead of showing it. The Result is vague ('a success', 'everyone was pleased') and gives no figures or lesson. Here is a better version: 'During half term the library had 200 books to return to the shelves by Monday morning, and two helpers were away. I was responsible for the children's section. I sorted the books into trolleys by shelf, put the picture books first because they were borrowed most, and checked each shelf against the list. I finished 90 books by Saturday lunchtime and the section was open on time. I learned to ask for a trolley rota earlier.' When you review a draft, list its errors in this way: wrong pronoun, missing part, vague verbs, claims without proof and weak Result.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with 'We worked hard and got everything done on time'?

options.text: It is written in the wrong tense for an example
It hides the writer's own part and names no specific action
It contains too much detail about the writer's actions
It includes a number that cannot be checked

questions.hint: 'We' and 'worked hard' do not show what the writer did.

questions.prompt: 'I think I am good at working under pressure' is a problem because it is what?

options.text: A Result that gives no figure or date at all
A Situation that is placed too late in the answer
A Task that has not been explained in enough detail
A claim about the writer rather than a shown action

questions.hint: Assessors score what you did, not what you claim.

questions.prompt: Which part of STAR is wholly missing from the weak sample?

options.text: The Result
The Task
The Situation
All of them

questions.hint: It never says what the writer had to finish.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with 'It was a success and everyone was pleased'?

options.text: It uses the word I too many times
It is untrue because the writer cannot know it
It is much too long for a Result
It is vague and gives no figures or lesson

questions.hint: A strong Result includes specifics and learning.

questions.prompt: In the better version, which sentence is the Task?

options.text: I sorted the books into trolleys by shelf.
I was responsible for the children's section.
I finished 90 books by Saturday lunchtime.
I learned to ask for a trolley rota earlier.

questions.hint: It says what the writer was responsible for.

questions.prompt: In the better version, why were picture books put first?

options.text: They were borrowed most, which shows a reasoned choice
They were the lightest to carry on the trolley
They were at the bottom of the list and needed doing
The library manager had asked for them to be done first

questions.hint: The reasoning shows effective prioritising.

questions.prompt: Which detail in the better version is the strongest evidence of Delivering at Pace?

options.text: The section opened on time, with 90 books done by Saturday
The writer volunteers at the library during the school holidays
The writer was responsible for the children's section of the library
The library had two helpers who were away for the half term

questions.hint: A deadline met with figures is the best evidence.

questions.prompt: Which list names the common errors in a draft?

options.text: Short sentences, plain words, numbers, good order and dates
Spelling, punctuation, capital letters and choice of font
Too many verbs, too many numbers and too much detail
Wrong pronoun, missing part, vague verbs, no proof, weak Result

questions.hint: These are the errors discussed in the passage.

questions.prompt: What does the better version learn at the end?

options.text: To stop sorting books into trolleys before a deadline
To ask for a trolley rota earlier
To work much more slowly so fewer books are missed
To avoid volunteering at busy times of the library year

questions.hint: The lesson is stated in the Result.

questions.prompt: Which weak phrase should be replaced with a specific verb?

options.text: Checked each shelf
Sorted the books
Worked hard
Finished 90 books

questions.hint: 'Worked hard' is vague and does not describe an action.

items.title: Level 4: Choosing the right example for the Behaviour
items.body: Choosing the right example is half the battle. Suppose the advert asks for Communicating and Influencing, and you have three stories. The first is about covering a colleague's shift. The second is about explaining a complicated benefit letter to an elderly neighbour in simple words and making sure she understood each step. The third is about finishing a big mailing before a deadline. The second is the best match, because the main action is explaining clearly and checking understanding. The first would suit Working Together, and the third would suit Delivering at Pace. This does not mean your stories can only fit one Behaviour. A strong story may show more than one, but you should choose it for the Behaviour where the main action matches the wording. Check the grade too. At Administrative Officer level, the description for Communicating and Influencing talks about listening, speaking and writing clearly and respectfully, and sharing information. An example about persuading a government minister would not match, and an example about writing a clear note for a team would. Finally, check that your example gives you enough to say. A story must have a Task, several Actions and a Result. If it is only a single moment, choose a fuller story. When you have several candidates, ask three questions: does the main action match the Behaviour, does it fit the grade, and is it rich enough to fill a STAR answer?

questions.prompt: The advert asks for Communicating and Influencing. Which story is the best match?

options.text: Finishing a large mailing in time for the afternoon post collection
Setting up a colour-coded folder system for a busy shared office
Explaining a benefit letter to a neighbour step by step
Covering a colleague's shift so she could attend a hospital visit

questions.hint: The main action is clear explanation and checking understanding.

questions.prompt: Covering a colleague's shift would best suit which Behaviour?

options.text: Communicating and Influencing
Making Effective Decisions
Seeing the Big Picture
Working Together

questions.hint: It shows cooperation and support.

questions.prompt: Finishing a big mailing before a deadline would best suit which Behaviour?

options.text: Delivering at Pace
Communicating and Influencing
Working Together
Developing Self and Others

questions.hint: It shows meeting a deadline.

questions.prompt: Why might an example about persuading a government minister be a poor match at AO level?

options.text: It uses too many names and job titles
It is far above the level described for the grade
It would be too short to make a full answer
Ministers cannot be mentioned in an application at all

questions.hint: The example should fit the grade.

questions.prompt: Which example fits the AO-level description of communicating?

options.text: Presenting findings to a full parliamentary committee
Negotiating a national contract with several large suppliers
Directing the work of a whole communications department
Writing a clear note for a team and checking it was understood

questions.hint: It is everyday and at the right level.

questions.prompt: What does 'rich enough' mean for an example?

options.text: It is long and takes several minutes to tell
It has a Task, several Actions and a Result
It comes from a paid job rather than a voluntary one
It involves well-known people or large organisations

questions.hint: A rich story can fill all STAR parts.

questions.prompt: Which of these examples is likely too thin to use?

options.text: A month spent organising a stall for a charity
A single phone call lasting a minute with no follow-up
A regular weekly volunteer role lasting a year
A six-week training course attended once a week

questions.hint: A single moment gives too little for STAR.

questions.prompt: What are the three questions to ask of a candidate example?

options.text: Is it recent, is it from a paid job, is it over a year long?
Did I win, did I lead, did I finish ahead of everyone?
Does the action match, fit the grade, and fill a STAR?
Is it well known, is it unusual, is it on a large scale?

questions.hint: These check fit, level and content.

questions.prompt: How should you use a story that shows more than one Behaviour?

options.text: Use identical wording for every Behaviour listed in the advert
Use it only when it comes from a paid job at a large employer
Use it for one Behaviour only and never again in the form
Choose it for the Behaviour where the main action fits

questions.hint: Stories can overlap, but build the answer around the main match.

questions.prompt: Which story best suits Delivering at Pace?

options.text: Welcoming a nervous new volunteer and showing the routine
Explaining a complicated letter to an elderly neighbour
Comparing three quotes for a repair and asking advice first
Ranking six tasks by urgency and finishing the top three before post time

questions.hint: Prioritising and meeting a deadline is Delivering at Pace.

items.title: Level 4: Ability tests, practice and fair adjustments
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: The Ability stage of an application is often an online test that must be completed by a set date. Some candidates worry because they have been out of education for years. There are a few facts worth knowing. The tests are designed to be fair and to measure aptitude, not school results. They are timed, so answering steadily matters more than perfecting one question. Wrong answers are not usually a reason to panic, since you can often still do well overall. In the verbal test, you judge a statement against a passage, using only the passage. In the numerical test, you read tables and charts and may need to work out totals, differences or percentages. In the judgement test, you choose the most and least effective responses to a work situation, which tends to reward honesty, fairness and teamwork. Preparation helps: sample tests are available on official sites, and doing a few helps you learn the layout and the pace. Doing them in a quiet place on a device with a good connection also matters. If you have a disability or a condition such as dyslexia that makes timed tests harder, you can ask for a reasonable adjustment, such as extra time. Ask as soon as you can, using the contact in the advert, because arrangements take time. You may be asked for evidence of your need. A request for an adjustment does not count against you.

questions.prompt: What do the Ability tests measure?

options.text: Your work history and the jobs you have held
Aptitude rather than school results
How well you did in exams at school years ago
The qualifications you gained at college or university

questions.hint: They are designed to measure aptitude.

questions.prompt: Why is steady answering sensible in a timed test?

options.text: Every wrong answer loses all the marks you have scored
Slow answers are automatically marked as incorrect
Only the first ten questions count towards the score
Time is limited, so one question can cost you others

questions.hint: Time management matters in timed tests.

questions.prompt: In which test do you judge statements using only a passage?

options.text: Verbal reasoning
Numerical reasoning
Technical
Judgement

questions.hint: Verbal reasoning uses a passage as the only source.

questions.prompt: In which test do you choose the most and least effective responses to a work situation?

options.text: The technical test
The judgement test
The verbal test
The numerical test

questions.hint: The judgement test uses situations with choices of response.

questions.prompt: What sort of responses does the judgement test tend to reward?

options.text: Staying silent
Honesty, fairness and teamwork
Loyalty to one friend above others
Speed and aggression

questions.hint: The Civil Service values underlie the test.

questions.prompt: Where can you find sample tests?

options.text: On official sites
In the Civil Service Code
Only from private tutors
Only at interview

questions.hint: Official sample tests are available.

questions.prompt: Why practise in a quiet place on a device with a good connection?

options.text: So that the connection speed is marked as part of the score
So that the test is made easier by the quiet conditions
So that you are not disrupted during the real test
So that you can skip questions without the system noticing

questions.hint: Good conditions avoid avoidable problems.

questions.prompt: Who can ask for a reasonable adjustment?

options.text: Only those with a medical letter at the time of applying
Only those with a degree
Only candidates who failed once
A person with a disability or condition such as dyslexia

questions.hint: Adjustments are for people whose condition makes the test harder.

questions.prompt: When should you ask for an adjustment?

options.text: Only at interview, when the panel asks if you need anything
On the day of the test, once you have seen the questions
After you have seen your results from the first stage
As soon as you can, using the contact in the advert

questions.hint: Early requests allow time to arrange it.

questions.prompt: Does asking for an adjustment count against you?

options.text: It lowers your score
It is noted at interview
It ends your application
It does not count against you

questions.hint: The request is a normal part of the process.

items.title: Level 4: Writing a Result with a number and a lesson
items.body: The Result is the shortest part of a STAR answer, but it turns a story into evidence. A good Result has three parts: what happened, how you know, and what you learned. What happened is the outcome. How you know is the number, date or reaction that proves it. What you learned is a short reflection. Compare three results to the same story about a school coffee morning. The first says: 'It went well.' It is true but gives nothing to score. The second says: 'We raised £320, which was £70 more than last year.' It has a number, but 'we' hides who did it. The third says: 'I raised £320, which was £70 more than last year, and the head teacher asked me to run it again. I learned to ask local shops for donations earlier.' It has the outcome, the evidence and the lesson, and it uses 'I'. If you do not have a number, use another kind of proof: a comment from a person, a repeat request, a deadline met or a complaint avoided. If something went wrong, say so briefly and say what you changed. That is honest and shows you learn. Do not claim results you did not achieve. If a team result depended on many people, say what your own contribution was, for example 'my stall took £90 of the total'. Keep the Result to two or three sentences, and make the last one the lesson.

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of a good Result?

options.text: What was planned, what was spent and what was left over
A claim, an opinion and a promise for the future
Who started it, who helped, and who finished it
What happened, how you know, and what you learned

questions.hint: These are the three parts described.

questions.prompt: Which Result is strongest?

options.text: Everyone who came on the morning said they had a nice time
We managed to raise a good amount of money for the school
I raised £320, £70 up on last year, and was asked to run it again
It all went very well and people seemed to enjoy themselves

questions.hint: It has outcome, evidence and a lesson in the first person.

questions.prompt: What is the weakness of 'We raised £320, which was £70 more than last year'?

options.text: It is much too long for a Result
It has no number to show how well it went
It has a number but does not show who did it
It is untrue because the writer did not raise it

questions.hint: 'We' hides your own part.

questions.prompt: What can you use as proof if you have no number?

options.text: A comment from a person or a repeat request
A longer description of the Situation before the Action
A statement listing the personal qualities you believe you have
A guess at a figure that sounds about right to you

questions.hint: Other evidence can stand in for a figure.

questions.prompt: What should you do if something went wrong?

options.text: Say so briefly and say what you changed
Leave it out so that the story sounds smoother
Describe it at length to show how hard it was
Blame the people who made the problem worse

questions.hint: Honest reflection shows you learn.

questions.prompt: How can you show your contribution to a team result?

options.text: Say that the team did everything and you simply took part
Say that you did everything yourself, so the credit is clear
Say what your own part produced, such as 'my stall took £90'
Avoid giving figures, because the team's total is what matters

questions.hint: Specify your own contribution.

questions.prompt: How long should the Result be?

options.text: As long as the Action
Two or three sentences
A full page
One word

questions.hint: It is the shortest part of the answer.

questions.prompt: What should the last sentence of the Result usually be?

options.text: The Situation
A promise to do better
The name of the manager
The lesson

questions.hint: Ending with the lesson shows reflection.

questions.prompt: Which of these is evidence that the Result was good?

options.text: The head teacher asked for it to be run again
The hall had been filled with chairs and tables
The writer felt very tired by the end of the day
The weather was sunny on the day of the fair

questions.hint: A repeat request is a form of proof.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with claiming a result you did not achieve?

options.text: It cannot be written down in the space on the form
Follow-up questions may expose it and it is dishonest
It makes the answer too short to be scored
It uses too many numbers for a short answer

questions.hint: Honesty is essential.

items.title: Level 4: Seeing the Big Picture compared with Managing a Quality Service
items.body: Imagine two people working on the same task, sending out benefit letters. Person One checks each address, spells each name correctly, uses the right template and ticks off each letter on a list. This is Managing a Quality Service, because the focus is accuracy and care for the customer. Person Two does all that, but also notices that many letters are sent on a Friday and arrive after the weekend, which delays people who rely on the money. She understands that the benefit helps people pay bills and so she suggests to her manager that the main batch be posted on Wednesday. Her thinking is Seeing the Big Picture, since she links her task to its effect on the public. Her suggestion is Changing and Improving, because she acts to improve things. All three Behaviours can be seen in one story, but a strong application chooses the one that matches the requirement. If the advert asks for Managing a Quality Service, put the weight on accuracy, checking and records. If it asks for Seeing the Big Picture, put the weight on how you understood the purpose, the people affected and why it mattered. Do not simply describe the task and hope the assessor will infer the Behaviour. Say what you realised, then what you did. Be careful not to turn an example about care into one about opinions.

questions.prompt: Person One checks addresses, names and templates and ticks off a list. Which Behaviour does she show most?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Changing and Improving
Delivering at Pace
Seeing the Big Picture

questions.hint: The focus is accuracy and care.

questions.prompt: Person Two notices Friday letters arrive after the weekend and delay payments. Which Behaviour does this noticing show?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Leadership
Developing Self and Others
Seeing the Big Picture

questions.hint: She links her task to its effect on the public.

questions.prompt: Person Two suggests posting the main batch on Wednesday. Which Behaviour does the suggestion show?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Communicating and Influencing
Changing and Improving
Working Together

questions.hint: She acts to improve how things are done.

questions.prompt: If the advert asks for Managing a Quality Service, where should the weight of the answer fall?

options.text: New ideas for posting
Accuracy, checking and records
Meeting deadlines
The wider purpose of the benefit

questions.hint: These are the focus of the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: If the advert asks for Seeing the Big Picture, where should the weight fall?

options.text: How many letters or forms you dealt with in total
How accurate each letter or form was when it left you
How you understood the purpose and the people affected
How fast you worked through the pile of tasks

questions.hint: This is the focus of the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of describing the task and hoping the assessor will infer the Behaviour?

options.text: The answer will probably run over the word limit
The assessor may not read as far as the Result
The assessor scores only what you say you did
The task may not be accepted as work experience

questions.hint: Assessors need explicit evidence.

questions.prompt: What should you say to show Seeing the Big Picture?

options.text: A list of all the tasks you were given that week
Your opinion of the department and how it is run
What you realised and then what you did
How many hours you worked on each of them

questions.hint: Realisation followed by action is the pattern.

questions.prompt: Why can one story show all three Behaviours?

options.text: Assessors give credit for all nine if a single one is shown
The three Behaviours are really just the same one named thrice
Real work involves care, understanding and improvement together
Stories are marked at random, so any one story can score

questions.hint: Real stories overlap.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion rather than evidence?

options.text: 'I think the department should always post on Wednesdays.'
'I suggested Wednesday posting to my manager in writing.'
'Letters then arrived before the weekend for most people.'
'I checked every name against the printed list before posting.'

questions.hint: Opinions are not actions or results.

questions.prompt: A benefit helps people pay their bills. Which Behaviour is shown by recognising this and letting it guide your work?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Leadership
Delivering at Pace
Developing Self and Others

questions.hint: Linking work to its effect on people is Seeing the Big Picture.

items.title: Level 4: Describing carer and parent experience for different requirements
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: The same home experience can be used for different requirements if you choose the right angle. Take a parent who runs a busy household with three children, one with additional needs. For a Managing a Quality Service requirement, she might write about keeping the child's medication log accurate and keeping school and clinic records so that nothing is missed. For a Delivering at Pace requirement, she might describe the morning routine: how she plans and prioritises the school run, a clinic visit and a work shift so that all are met on time. For a Communicating and Influencing requirement, she might describe a meeting with school staff where she explained her child's needs clearly and agreed a plan. For a Working Together requirement, she might describe agreeing a rota with her partner and a neighbour. The facts are all true, but the angle differs. For an Experience requirement such as 'dealing with the public', she could describe her dealings with teachers, doctors and officials. It is important to give real numbers where possible, such as the number of children, the number of appointments each month or the number of years. It is also important not to claim too much. Parenting is not a job title. Describe the tasks, the responsibility and the outcome, using the plain language of work, and let the assessor decide what the experience is worth.

questions.prompt: For a Managing a Quality Service requirement, which angle suits the parent best?

options.text: Keeping an accurate medication log and records so nothing is missed
Explaining the child's needs clearly at a meeting with the school
Agreeing a shared rota for lifts with a neighbour and a partner
Describing how the school-run routine is planned to keep to time

questions.hint: Accuracy and records fit quality of service.

questions.prompt: For a Delivering at Pace requirement, which angle suits best?

options.text: Planning the morning so the school run, clinic and shift all run on time
Keeping an accurate medication log and clinic records for the child
Explaining the child's needs clearly at a meeting with school staff
Agreeing a shared rota for lifts with a partner and a neighbour

questions.hint: Planning to meet times is Delivering at Pace.

questions.prompt: For Communicating and Influencing, which angle suits best?

options.text: Keeping the child's clinic and school records in good order
Agreeing a rota for childcare with a partner and a neighbour
Planning and prioritising the school run, clinic visit and shift
Explaining her child's needs clearly to school staff

questions.hint: Clear explanation to reach an agreement is communicating and influencing.

questions.prompt: For Working Together, which angle suits best?

options.text: Explaining the child's needs to school staff and agreeing a plan
Agreeing a rota with her partner and a neighbour
Keeping an accurate medication log and clinic appointments diary
Planning and prioritising the morning routine so all is on time

questions.hint: Sharing duties by agreement is Working Together.

questions.prompt: For an Experience requirement of 'dealing with the public', which activity could she describe?

options.text: Her morning routine of getting the children ready for school
Her cooking for the family on most evenings of the week
Her hobbies at home, such as sewing and baking
Her dealings with teachers, doctors and officials

questions.hint: These are dealings with other people and officials.

questions.prompt: Which detail would make a parent's example stronger?

options.text: The number of children, appointments each month and years of caring
A claim that she is a natural leader in her family
A statement that bringing up children is hard work for anyone
An apology that she has not held a paid job for some years

questions.hint: Real numbers make it specific.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid claiming too much about parenting?

options.text: Parenting is not a job title, so describe tasks and outcomes
Parenting rarely shows any of the Behaviours at all
Parenting is private and best left out of applications
Parenting is not accepted as evidence by assessors

questions.hint: Describe the facts and let the assessor judge.

questions.prompt: How can one piece of home experience support different requirements?

options.text: Use identical wording each time, whatever the requirement says
Choose the angle that matches each requirement
Use it once only and find new experience for the other parts
Use it only if the activity was paid at some point in the past

questions.hint: Different aspects can support different requirements.

questions.prompt: What language should the parent use?

options.text: Informal slang that sounds friendly and relaxed
The plain language of work
Medical terms that show knowledge of the child's needs
Legal wording that makes the account sound official

questions.hint: Plain, work-style language works best.

questions.prompt: What should the parent give besides the task and responsibility?

options.text: The outcome
A complaint
A promise
An apology

questions.hint: Outcome completes the evidence.

items.title: Level 4: Preparing a set of examples for an AO application
items.body: A good set of examples saves time and improves quality. Aim for a bank of six to eight real stories that you have written down in STAR form, each about 150 to 250 words. Spread them across different areas of life. Try to have two from paid work or study, two from home or family, and two from volunteering or the community, if you can. For each story, note which Behaviours it could support. A single story may be tagged with two or three. Then, when an advert arrives, match stories to the Behaviours it lists. Avoid using the same story for every Behaviour, because assessors read your whole application and repeated stories look thin. If the form allows only a limited number of words per answer, write the full version first and then cut it, keeping the Action and Result. Keep a short version of about 60 words for use in a spoken interview as an opening, and be ready to add detail if asked. Update the bank when you do something new. Do not forget to record dates and names. For an interview, say the stories aloud with a friend or alone, so that you hear where you stumble. Remember that you are not memorising a script, but becoming comfortable with the facts. If you are asked a question that does not match any story exactly, choose the closest and adapt the emphasis, not the facts.

questions.prompt: How many stories does the passage suggest keeping in your bank?

options.text: Six to eight
Twenty to thirty
One
Two

questions.hint: A bank of six to eight gives enough choice.

questions.prompt: Roughly how long should each written story be?

options.text: 1,000 words
20 words
150 to 250 words
Three pages

questions.hint: The suggested length is 150 to 250 words.

questions.prompt: Why spread the stories across different areas of life?

options.text: So that the application form looks longer and more complete
So you have a range of evidence and avoid repeating one story
So that you can avoid giving much detail in any one story
So that all of the stories can be about your paid work

questions.hint: Variety stops the application looking thin.

questions.prompt: Why avoid using the same story for every Behaviour?

options.text: Assessors read the whole application and repetition looks thin
It uses up more words than separate stories would need
It takes up too much of the time you have for the form
It is banned by the rules on the Civil Service Jobs site

questions.hint: Repeated stories look weak.

questions.prompt: What should you do if the form has a tight word limit?

options.text: Write the full version first, then cut it, keeping Action and Result
Cut the Result first, as the assessor can usually infer it
Cut the Action first, as it takes up the most words in the answer
Keep only the Situation and Task, which set the scene for the reader

questions.hint: Cutting from a full version keeps the key parts.

questions.prompt: How long might a short spoken version be?

options.text: About 600 words
About five words
About 60 words
About a page

questions.hint: A short opening version can be about 60 words.

questions.prompt: Why say stories aloud before an interview?

options.text: To memorise a script
To remove the Result
To make them longer
To hear where you stumble

questions.hint: Speaking aloud shows weak spots.

questions.prompt: What should you do if no story exactly matches the question?

options.text: Make up a story that fits the question exactly
Choose the closest and adapt the emphasis, not the facts
Use a story that a friend told you about their work
Say that you cannot answer and move on to the next

questions.hint: Emphasis can change, facts must not.

questions.prompt: Why tag each story with Behaviours?

options.text: So that they can be handed to the panel as a contents page
Because the application form asks for the tags to be listed
So you can match stories quickly to an advert
So the stories look neat when they are written down

questions.hint: Tags help you pick stories fast.

questions.prompt: When should you update the bank of stories?

options.text: Only after an interview
Only once a year
Never
Whenever you do something new

questions.hint: Keeping it current adds fresh evidence.

items.title: Level 4: Honesty, exaggeration and follow-up questions
items.body: Honesty runs through every part of a Civil Service application. The Civil Service Code lists honesty and integrity among its values, and applicants are expected to give a true account of themselves. Exaggeration is more tempting than outright lies, and it is harder to spot in your own writing. Examples include turning 'I helped a little' into 'I led', claiming a team result as your own, giving a figure that is rounded up or saying you have a qualification you are still working on. In an application, false information may lead to the offer being withdrawn, even after a start. An interviewer who suspects an example is exaggerated will usually ask follow-ups such as 'Who else was involved?', 'What did you do first?', 'What went wrong?' and 'What would you do differently?' A truthful story can answer these easily, since you lived it. An exaggerated story tends to fall apart. Being honest does not mean being modest to the point of hiding what you did. State your actions clearly and specifically, but name the contribution of others where it happened. If you are unsure of a figure, say 'about'. If something went wrong, say so and describe how you responded. An honest example with a small result is far better than an inflated one with a large result that cannot be explained. Panels respect candidates who admit a mistake and show what they learned.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of exaggeration?

options.text: Turning 'I helped a little' into 'I led'
Naming the colleagues who also worked on the project
Stating plainly what went wrong and how it was fixed
Saying 'about £300' when you cannot recall the exact sum

questions.hint: It overstates the role actually played.

questions.prompt: What can happen if false information is found in an application?

options.text: The offer may be withdrawn, even after a start
Nothing, as long as the answer was short
A warning only at interview
A small score reduction

questions.hint: False information can lead to offers being withdrawn.

questions.prompt: Which follow-up question tests whether you worked alone?

options.text: Where did you go to school?
How old are you?
Who else was involved?
What is your favourite colour?

questions.hint: It probes the role of others.

questions.prompt: Why does a truthful story hold up under follow-ups?

options.text: It is usually shorter than an invented one
You lived it and can answer from memory
It has been rehearsed many times beforehand
It has more numbers in it than a made-up one

questions.hint: Real events are easy to describe in detail.

questions.prompt: How should honesty and modesty work together in an answer?

options.text: State your actions clearly and name others' contributions
Be honest by claiming the whole result, even if others helped
Be honest in writing, and relaxed about the details in speech
Be modest by leaving out your own part and naming only the team

questions.hint: Be clear about yourself without overclaiming.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to treat a figure you are unsure of?

options.text: Pick a figure that sounds right and use it throughout
Round it up so that it sounds more impressive
Say 'about' and give the nearest figure
Leave the figure out and describe the result in words

questions.hint: Honest approximations are fine.

questions.prompt: Which is better, an honest small result or an inflated large result you cannot explain?

options.text: The inflated result
They are equal
Neither
The honest small result

questions.hint: Credibility matters more than size.

questions.prompt: How do panels tend to view a candidate who admits a mistake and says what was learned?

options.text: As a poor communicator
With suspicion
With respect
As unsuitable

questions.hint: Honest reflection is valued.

questions.prompt: Where does the Civil Service Code list honesty?

options.text: Among the five elements
Among its values
In the Success Profiles test
Among the nine Behaviours

questions.hint: Honesty and integrity are Civil Service values.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of exaggeration about qualifications?

options.text: Saying you hope to gain one if the job requires it
Saying you are currently studying for one and expect to finish
Saying you hold one you are still working towards
Saying you have applied to take an exam in the coming year

questions.hint: Claiming something unfinished as held is false.

items.title: Level 4: Reading Behaviour wording at Administrative Officer level
items.body: The published Behaviour descriptions for the lowest levels use plain statements, and it helps to turn each into a question you can answer with a story. For Communicating and Influencing, the descriptions talk about listening to others, communicating clearly in speech and writing, and treating people with respect. A question to ask yourself is: when did I explain something clearly to someone who needed it? For Working Together, the descriptions talk about building positive relationships, sharing information and respecting different views. The question is: when did I help a group get something done or make someone feel included? For Delivering at Pace, the descriptions talk about working to deadlines, using time well, and taking responsibility for your own work. The question is: when did I finish something important on time despite pressure? For Managing a Quality Service, the descriptions talk about following procedures, being accurate and treating customers well. The question is: when did I make sure something was right? For Seeing the Big Picture, the question is: when did I understand why my work mattered? For Changing and Improving: when did I suggest or try a better way? For Making Effective Decisions: when did I use facts and advice to choose? For Leadership: when did I set a positive example? For Developing Self and Others: when did I learn or teach something? Use these questions as prompts when you search your memory for stories.

questions.prompt: Which question prompts a story for Delivering at Pace?

options.text: When did I explain something difficult to someone clearly?
When did I suggest a better way of doing a regular job?
When did I learn something new and then pass it on?
When did I finish something important on time despite pressure?

questions.hint: It targets deadlines and pressure.

questions.prompt: Which question prompts a story for Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: When did I make sure something was right?
When did I make someone feel included?
When did I set a positive example?
When did I use advice to choose?

questions.hint: It targets accuracy and care.

questions.prompt: Which question prompts a story for Changing and Improving?

options.text: When did I check each detail until I was sure it was right?
When did I help a colleague who was short of time?
When did I suggest or try a better way?
When did I finish something important on time despite pressure?

questions.hint: It targets improvements.

questions.prompt: Which question prompts a story for Seeing the Big Picture?

options.text: When did I explain clearly?
When did I learn something?
When did I help a group get something done?
When did I understand why my work mattered?

questions.hint: It targets understanding of purpose.

questions.prompt: Which question prompts a story for Making Effective Decisions?

options.text: When did I meet a tight deadline under some pressure?
When did I explain a letter to someone who needed it?
When did I set a positive example for people around me?
When did I use facts and advice to choose?

questions.hint: It targets sensible choices.

questions.prompt: Which question prompts a story for Leadership?

options.text: When did I set a positive example?
When did I explain a letter?
When did I use facts to choose?
When did I check accuracy?

questions.hint: It targets example and attitude.

questions.prompt: Which question prompts a story for Developing Self and Others?

options.text: When did I learn or teach something?
When did I suggest a better way?
When did I finish early?
When did I follow a procedure?

questions.hint: It targets learning and teaching.

questions.prompt: Which question prompts a story for Working Together?

options.text: When did I rank my tasks by urgency to meet a deadline?
When did I check a record until I was sure it was right?
When did I help a group get something done or include someone?
When did I compare two options before I made a choice?

questions.hint: It targets cooperation and inclusion.

questions.prompt: What do the lowest-level descriptions for Communicating and Influencing mention?

options.text: Writing long policy papers for senior colleagues
Briefing ministers on the progress of a project
Negotiating contracts with suppliers and partners
Listening, clear speech and writing, and respect

questions.hint: These are the entry-level descriptions.

questions.prompt: Why turn each description into a question?

options.text: It makes the descriptions shorter and easier to learn
The panel will ask you exactly those questions
It prompts you to recall real stories from your memory
The application form requires those questions to be answered

questions.hint: Questions are useful memory prompts.
